passage:
Wednesday. They did it again in the lunch line: 'Hum jaayenge, hum khaayenge,' copying the way I talk, Nitin loudest. Everyone laughed. For a month I've been answering in class with one word so nobody hears my accent. Today I noticed I hadn't said a full sentence all day. That felt worse than the teasing. So after sixth period I went to Kulkarni sir and told him it's been every day since August. He wrote down the names and dates I remembered, thanked me for telling him, and spoke to Nitin's group before the last bell. He said if it happens again, come straight to him. Then Aparna from debate club caught me at the gate. 'Join us Friday. You argue better than half the team, accent and all.' I laughed out loud for the first time in weeks. Maybe I don't have to shrink.
- Vishal

qa.q: What did the group copy in the lunch line?
qa.a: The way Vishal talks: 'Hum jaayenge, hum khaayenge'.

qa.q: How was Vishal feeling after noticing no full sentence had been spoken all day?
qa.a: Vishal felt worse than during the teasing, sad and ashamed at having shrunk so much.

qa.q: Which step helped Vishal most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Kulkarni sir with names and dates, because the teacher acted the same day and offered to step in again.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Vishal's way of speaking?
qa.a: Aparna values Vishal's arguments and treats the accent as no problem at all, just part of who Vishal is.

grounding: A diary showing a teen teased for an accent who stops shrinking, tells a teacher and finds a club that values them as they are.

passage: Pankaj had been dreading his first week at Sunrise Public School in Andheri. He was repeating Class 10, a year older than everyone, and he'd heard the whispers in the corridor: 'That's the one who failed.' On Thursday he hovered at the door of the robotics lab. Gopika Ma'am looked up from a tangle of wires. 'Pankaj, right? Good, I need someone with steady hands. Can you solder?' Nobody asked about last year. By five o'clock he'd fixed a motor and laughed twice. On the bus home he leaned his head against the window and felt his shoulders drop for the first time in months. Three weeks later, a thin new boy stood frozen at the same lab door, clutching his bag. Pankaj waved him in. 'Come, we need steady hands.'

qa.q: What did Gopika Ma'am ask Pankaj at the lab door?
qa.a: Whether he could solder, because she needed someone with steady hands.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's dropping shoulders on the bus suggest?
qa.a: It suggests deep relief after months of tension about being judged for repeating a year 🙂

qa.q: How did Pankaj pay the kindness forward?
qa.a: He waved in a frozen new boy using the same welcoming words he had heard.

qa.q: How does Gopika Ma'am see Pankaj when he arrives?
qa.a: She sees a useful new pair of hands, not the student who failed, and welcomes him without questions.

grounding: Shows a teen repeating a year who is welcomed without judgment by a club teacher, feels relief and passes on the welcome.

passage:
'I... I wanted to try for the p-play,' Bhupen said, eyes on the floor of the hall.
'Great. Take a script,' said Charu, the drama club captain, sliding one across the stage.
'You heard me, right? I st-stammer.'
'I heard. Page four. Read the grandfather. He's grumpy, you'll love him.'
Bhupen read. It took a while. Nobody giggled. When he finished, Charu clapped once. 'You pause before the angry lines. That's actually perfect for him.'
'You're not just being nice?'
'I'm the captain. I'm never just nice. Ask anyone.'
Somebody at the back laughed. 'She's really not.'
Bhupen laughed too, and something in his chest unknotted.
'Rehearsals are Tuesday and Friday,' Charu said. 'And stay back next week? Help me with the new kids' auditions.'
'Me?'
'You know exactly how scary that door is.'

qa.q: Which part did Charu ask Bhupen to read?
qa.a: The grandfather, on page four.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel after nobody giggled at his reading?
qa.a: He felt deep relief, as something in his chest unknotted and he laughed along.

qa.q: Why is Charu's request about auditions a good idea?
qa.a: It lets Bhupen pay the welcome forward to new kids, since he knows how scary that door is.

qa.q: How does Charu see Bhupen's stammer?
qa.a: She sees it as no barrier, even noticing his pauses suit the grumpy grandfather.

grounding: Shows a teen who stammers being welcomed by a drama club without judgment, feeling relief and being invited to welcome others.

passage: Teacher's note, Culture Week, Grade 9. Manjula's stall today was the busiest in the hall. She had brought her Ajji's kasuti embroidery, written everyone's names in Kannada script on little cards, and explained each festival dish with real pride. When Sumit from the next stall joked that 'your lot only eat ragi balls', she didn't snap back or mock his food in return. She laughed, handed him a card with his name in Kannada, and asked about the Garhwali song playing at his stall. He ended up teaching her the chorus while she taught him how to say 'thank you' in Kannada. Later she told me, 'I love where I'm from. That doesn't mean his place is worse.' I've asked her to help plan next year's exchange between the two sections.

qa.q: What did Manjula write on the little cards?
qa.a: Everyone's names in Kannada script.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling while explaining the festival dishes?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy to share her culture, which is why she explained each dish with real pride 😊

qa.q: What did Manjula's response to Sumit's joke get right?
qa.a: She stayed proud without putting his culture down, and turned the joke into curiosity by asking about his song.

qa.q: How might Sumit see the moment Manjula handed him the card?
qa.a: He likely felt surprised and welcomed rather than attacked, which is why he taught her the chorus.

grounding: A teacher's note showing a teen proud of her language and culture who stays curious about a classmate's and puts no one down.

passage:
Saturday night. Went to Irfan's for Eid lunch today. Before that, in the class group, everyone was fighting about which state has the best food, and I had typed a whole paragraph about why Konkani fish curry beats everything, plus a meme making fun of Hyderabadi biryani. I love our food. I love that Aaji still sings in Konkani while she cooks and that I can answer her. That's mine and I'm proud of it. But I deleted the meme before sending. It felt like it needed Irfan's food to lose for mine to win, and that's not what I feel. At lunch I asked Irfan's Ammi how the haleem is made, and she talked for twenty minutes, so happy. I told them about Aaji's songs. Irfan wants to come for Ganpati now. Proud and curious, both.
- Chinmay

qa.q: What did Chinmay delete before sending?
qa.a: A meme making fun of Hyderabadi biryani.

qa.a: She felt happy and valued, talking for twenty minutes about her cooking 😊

grounding: A diary showing a teen proud of their language and food who stays curious about a friend's culture instead of putting it down.

passage: Emeka noticed that Beatriz, the new girl in his Year 10 class in Leicester, always arrived smelling faintly of oranges and fell asleep in first-period maths. Some of the lads joked she partied all night. Emeka wasn't sure. At lunch he sat down across from her. 'Can I ask something? You don't have to answer. You always look knackered in the mornings.' Beatriz hesitated, then shrugged. 'I help my avó set up her fruit stall at the market. Five o'clock, every day.' 'Every day? Before school?' She nodded. He wanted to say 'that's mad', but he kept quiet and listened instead. She told him about the stall, about arriving from Portugal last year, about how cold the mornings were. Emeka thought of his own mornings, cereal and a lift from Dad. On Friday he saved her the seat by the radiator.

qa.q: What does Beatriz do before school every day?
qa.a: She helps her avó set up her fruit stall at the market.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he nearly said 'that's mad'?
qa.a: He felt surprised and curious, but held back so he could listen rather than judge.

qa.q: What made Emeka's approach respectful?
qa.a: He asked gently, said she didn't have to answer, and listened instead of assuming like the others.

qa.q: How might Beatriz see Emeka's question at lunch?
qa.a: She may have felt wary at first, then relieved that someone asked instead of joking that she partied all night.

grounding: Shows a teen curious about a classmate's very different life who asks respectfully, listens rather than assumes and learns from it.

passage: On the second night of the state science camp, held in a college hostel in Raipur, Chandrika found herself on dish duty with Lalit. He had barely spoken all day. She'd heard someone say he was 'from a jungle village', and she had already pictured mud huts and no electricity. Instead of guessing, she asked, 'Where's home for you?' 'A village near Kondagaon. I walk to school, nearly an hour each way.' 'An hour? What do you do on the walk?' He smiled for the first time. 'Revise out loud. In Gondi, then Hindi.' She had never met anyone who thought in three languages. 'Can you teach me how you'd say "water"?' He did, laughing at her accent. By the time the plates were stacked, Chandrika knew his school had one science teacher and that he'd built his project from a broken torch. She stopped picturing and started listening.

qa.q: How long is Lalit's walk to school?
qa.a: Nearly an hour each way.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's question about the walk suggest about her?
qa.a: She felt genuinely curious and interested, moving past the picture she had assumed.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do instead of trusting the gossip?
qa.a: She asked Lalit directly and respectfully, then listened and asked to learn a Gondi word.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Chandrika's questions on dish duty?
qa.a: He seems pleased and more at ease, smiling for the first time and laughing at her accent.

grounding: Shows a teen meeting a classmate from a very different life, asking respectfully, listening instead of assuming, and learning from him.

passage: The project was due at nine the next morning, and the only free computer in the school library belonged to Harish's group. Lavanya needed it for twenty minutes. 'Ask your mother to buy you one,' Harish said loudly. 'Oh wait, she cleans houses, na?' Two boys snorted. Lavanya's face went hot. She felt about two inches tall and furious at once, and wanted to throw the chart paper at him. Instead she breathed, picked up her bag and said, 'My mother works harder than anyone in this room.' The librarian had stepped out and the bell was about to ring, so Lavanya walked straight to the staffroom and told Mr Thomas exactly what Harish had said. He wrote it down, told her the remark showed Harish's prejudice, not anything true about her, called Harish in before he could leave, and booked her a library slot before school. Her friend Divya was waiting outside to walk home with her.

qa.q: What did Harish say about Lavanya's mother?
qa.a: He said she cleans houses, after telling Lavanya to ask her mother to buy a computer.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when the boys snorted?
qa.a: She felt small, about two inches tall, and furious at the same time.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that was wise under the time pressure?
qa.a: She stood up for her mother calmly, left instead of throwing anything, and reported it to a teacher right away.

qa.q: How does Harish seem to see Lavanya's family?
qa.a: He looks down on them because of her mother's work, a bias that says more about him than about Lavanya.

grounding: Shows a teen mocked about her family's income who feels small and angry, reports it to a teacher and stays with a friend who respects her.

passage: The results for the maths olympiad were pinned outside the staffroom in Secunderabad, and Kishore's name was second from the top. Uday read it, then said, loud enough for the corridor, 'Must be nice. Your lot get everything on quota anyway.' A few people went quiet. Kishore's ears rang. For a second he felt tiny, as if the paper could blow his name away. Then anger came up hot behind it. He wanted to shove Uday. He didn't. His friends Farhan and Deepa stepped close on either side. 'He topped the mock tests all term,' Deepa said flatly. 'Everyone saw.' At lunch Kishore went to Mrs Joseph, the class teacher, and repeated Uday's words exactly. She said the remark came from Uday's prejudice, not from anything about Kishore's ability, and sent for Uday that afternoon. Walking home, Farhan and Deepa kept talking about the next round, as if the remark didn't deserve the space.

qa.q: Where were the olympiad results pinned?
qa.a: Outside the staffroom in Secunderabad.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling right after Uday's remark?
qa.a: He felt tiny at first, then hot anger rose up behind it.

qa.q: What steps helped Kishore handle the remark?
qa.a: He didn't shove Uday, stayed with friends who backed him, and told the class teacher Uday's exact words.

qa.q: How do Farhan and Deepa see Uday's remark?
qa.a: They see it as unfair bias against a friend who earned his place, so they stand close and move on to the next round.

grounding: Shows a teen hit by a caste-based remark who feels small and angry, reports it to a teacher and stays with friends who respect him.

passage: At the government school in Barnala, the new rule said only boys could use the computer room after classes; girls had to go straight home 'for safety'. Simran was furious. Her typing test for the district scholarship was a month away. Arohi wanted to shout at the peon who locked the door on them. Simran grabbed her arm. 'Shouting gets us nowhere. Let's write everything down.' For two weeks they noted each day: the date, how many boys used the room, the time the girls were turned away. Their Hindi teacher, Mrs Kaur, agreed it was unfair and helped them draft a letter. Twelve girls signed it. They submitted it to the School Management Committee, and Simran's mother, who sat on the committee, made sure it was read at the next meeting. The rule changed to a shared timetable, with a teacher present for everyone.

qa.q: What test was Simran preparing for?
qa.a: A typing test for the district scholarship, a month away.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling about the new rule, and how did she use it?
qa.a: She felt furious, but she channelled that anger into careful record-keeping instead of shouting.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Writing down dates and times, getting a teacher's help and sending a signed letter to the committee, because facts and a formal route were hard to ignore.

qa.q: How might the School Management Committee have seen the girls' letter?
qa.a: As clear evidence of an unfair rule, backed by twelve signatures and a teacher, so it had to act.

grounding: Shows teens facing an unfair school rule who record facts, find a teacher ally and use a formal complaint, channelling their anger.

passage: The new sign by the climbing wall at Astrid's school in Aarhus said: 'Not for students using mobility aids.' Astrid, who had climbed with an adapted harness at the city club for two years, read it three times. Her hands shook with anger. Emil, beside her, muttered, 'That's ridiculous.' 'It is,' she said. 'So let's prove it.' That evening she photographed the sign, wrote down the date, and asked her club coach for a letter explaining how the harness worked safely. Emil collected signatures from the class. Their form tutor, Mr Larsen, showed them the school's official complaints form and checked their wording. Astrid wrote: 'This rule treats a whole group of students as unsafe without looking at any of us.' Two weeks later the head teacher replied: the sign would come down, and the gym would be assessed with the club's help. Astrid still felt angry. But now she knew what to do with it.

qa.q: What did the new sign by the climbing wall say?
qa.a: 'Not for students using mobility aids.'

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling when she read the sign three times?
qa.a: She was angry enough that her hands shook, but she turned that anger into a plan.

qa.q: What made Astrid's complaint hard to ignore?
qa.a: She documented the sign and date, got a letter from her coach, gathered signatures and used the official form 👍

qa.q: How does Emil see the rule?
qa.a: He thinks it is ridiculous and unfair to Astrid, so he helps by collecting signatures.

grounding: Shows a teen facing an unfair school rule against students using mobility aids who documents facts, finds allies and uses the formal complaint route.

passage: First day of term. When Kashish, the new boy from Manipur, sat beside him, Yogesh caught himself thinking the thing his uncles always joked about at home: 'Those people just party, they don't study.' He shifted his bag to the far side of the desk. Three weeks later. Kashish solved the physics problem nobody else could and then, at lunch, stayed back to explain it to Yogesh twice, patiently. Walking home, Yogesh felt his face burn. 'I believed a joke about someone I'd never met,' he muttered. That night he felt awful, like a bad person. Then he wrote in his notebook: 'Not bad. Just learned it wrong. Can relearn.' Two months later. At a family dinner, Chacha started the same joke. Yogesh said quietly, 'My physics partner is from Manipur. He's the smartest guy in class.' Chacha frowned, but didn't finish the joke.

qa.q: What did Kashish do at lunch three weeks into term?
qa.a: He stayed back to explain the physics problem to Yogesh twice, patiently.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, his face burning, realising he had believed a joke about someone he'd never met.

qa.q: How did Yogesh avoid falling into self-hate?
qa.a: He named the stereotype, then wrote that he wasn't bad, just taught wrong, and could relearn 🙂

qa.q: How might Chacha see Yogesh's comment at dinner?
qa.a: He may feel surprised or challenged, frowning, but it was enough to make him stop the joke.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing a stereotype absorbed at home, meeting a real person from that group and unlearning it gradually without self-hate.

passage: Ojas, you asked why Salma Aunty is at every family function. Let me tell you something I'm not proud of. When I was fifteen in Belgaum, my family said things at dinner about 'those people' in the mohalla: dirty, dangerous, not like us. I believed every word. When Salma joined my class, I wouldn't share a bench with her. Then we were put together for the science fair. She came to our house with her father's old radio to take apart, and she was funny, and kind, and her tiffin was the best thing I'd ever tasted. I lay awake that night feeling sick at what I'd been thinking. But my own Ajji told me, 'You learned it, you can unlearn it. Slowly. Just don't stop.' It took years, Ojas. Salma is still my closest friend. That's how your Kalyani Aaji learned it.

qa.q: What did Salma bring to Kalyani's house for the science fair?
qa.a: Her father's old radio to take apart.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel lying awake that night?
qa.a: Kalyani felt sick with guilt and shame about the things she had believed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Kalyani's story?
qa.a: Being paired with Salma for the science fair and getting to know her as a real, funny, kind person.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when Kalyani refused to share a bench?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and unwelcome, judged before Kalyani even knew her.

grounding: An elder's story of noticing prejudice absorbed at home, getting to know a real person and unlearning it slowly without self-hate.

passage:
Monday night. I'm still annoyed at myself. On the bus today Varun said to Ritu, 'Go back to Bihar, you people take all our seats,' and a few of them laughed. Ritu just looked out of the window. My heart was going so fast. I wanted to say something, but my mouth wouldn't open. I kept thinking, what if they turn on me. Two stops later I finally said, 'That's not okay,' kind of quietly. Varun rolled his eyes but stopped. It wasn't much. After school I messaged Ritu: 'Sorry I took so long. What he said was rubbish. You okay?' She replied, 'Honestly, you saying anything helped. Thanks.' At dinner I told Mummy. She said I'd done the right thing and helped me email Sinha ma'am tonight, since it's the third time. Tomorrow I'm sitting next to Ritu on the bus.
- Kishore

qa.q: What did Kishore finally say to Varun?
qa.a: 'That's not okay,' kind of quietly.

qa.q: Why did Kishore hesitate to speak up?
qa.a: Kishore felt scared, heart racing, worried the group would turn on Kishore next.

qa.q: What small steps did Kishore take that mattered?
qa.a: Saying 'that's not okay', messaging Ritu afterwards, and getting an adult's help to report it.

qa.q: How did Ritu experience Kishore speaking up?
qa.a: She said it helped, so she felt less alone even though the words came late and quietly.

grounding: A diary showing a teen hesitating when a friend faces a bigoted remark, then taking a small stand and checking on her later.

passage: When Ojas came to drop off the chemistry notes, Nikita's Masi was visiting from Ahmedabad. After he left, she wrinkled her nose. 'That boy's family eats meat, na? And they're from that community. Don't keep too close, beta. People talk.' Nikita's Nani nodded along. Nikita felt her chest tighten. She wanted to snap, but she set down the tea tray first. 'Masi, Ojas is the one who stayed after class for a week to help me pass chemistry. His family eating differently doesn't make him less.' Masi clicked her tongue. 'You'll understand when you're older.' 'Maybe. But I'm not dropping a good friend.' Later, Nikita's mother squeezed her shoulder in the kitchen. 'Masi grew up with those ideas for fifty years. She won't change in one evening. Keep being polite, and keep your friend.' Nikita nodded. The next Sunday, she invited Ojas for lunch anyway.

qa.q: Why had Ojas come to Nikita's house?
qa.a: To drop off the chemistry notes.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when Masi told her not to keep too close?

qa.q: What went right in how Nikita disagreed with Masi?
qa.a: She spoke calmly and respectfully, gave a real example of Ojas's kindness, and made clear she wouldn't drop him.

qa.q: How does Masi seem to see Ojas?
qa.a: She judges him by his family's community and food, not by who he is, holding ideas she grew up with.

passage:
'That Vinita girl was here again?' Dadi asked, lowering herself onto the divan.
'Yes, Dadi. We're doing the history project together.'
'Their people are different, Zainab. They don't understand our ways. Find a friend from our side.'
Zainab put down her pencil. 'Dadi, can I tell you something about her?'
'Tell.'
'When you were in hospital last year, who do you think brought me notes every single day so I didn't fall behind?'
Dadi was quiet.
'Vinita. Every day, on her cycle, in the rain.'
'Hmph. One good deed.'
'A hundred good deeds, Dadi. I love you. But I'm keeping her.'
Ammi, from the kitchen doorway, said softly, 'Give Dadi time, Zainab.'
'I will. I'm not in a hurry.'
Dadi picked up her tasbih. After a long pause she said, 'Next time she comes, bring her to say salaam.'

qa.q: What did Vinita bring Zainab when Dadi was in hospital?
qa.a: Notes, every single day, on her cycle, in the rain.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she told Dadi 'I'm keeping her'?
qa.a: She felt loving but firm, hurt by Dadi's words yet steady in her loyalty to Vinita.

qa.q: Why was Zainab's reply to Ammi a wise one?
qa.a: Saying she's not in a hurry accepts that Dadi's views will change slowly, without giving up the friendship.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Vinita by the end?
qa.a: She is still wary but softening enough to want Vinita brought to say salaam 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen respectfully disagreeing with an elder who looks down on her friend's community, keeping the friend and giving the elder time.

passage: Vikas's family had moved from Gaya to Bengaluru in the middle of term, and exams started in his second week. He didn't know a word of Kannada, and the boys at the back mimicked his Hindi, 'Kya re, sattu boy?', after they saw his tiffin. On the day of the Kannada oral, the power went out, the fans stopped, and he stood sweating at the board, forgetting even the greeting he'd practised. Laughter. He sat down, cheeks burning, thinking of his old school, where everyone knew his name. At lunch Yash, who had moved from Pune two years earlier, slid along the bench. 'I was the "Marathi boy" for a whole year. I'll teach you ten useful Kannada words, and you teach me what sattu actually is.' Vikas laughed. That evening Maa packed extra sattu: one tiffin for him, one for Yash.

qa.q: What happened during Vikas's Kannada oral?
qa.a: The power went out, the fans stopped, and he forgot even the greeting he'd practised.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he sat down after the oral?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and homesick, cheeks burning, missing his old school where everyone knew his name.

qa.q: What small step helped Vikas start to belong?
qa.a: Accepting Yash's offer to swap Kannada words for sattu, which keeps his roots while he learns local ways.

qa.q: How does Yash see Vikas's struggle?
qa.a: He recognises it from his own year as the 'Marathi boy', so he offers friendship and help.

grounding: Shows a teen who moved cities and is teased for his language and food, keeping his roots while finding an ally and learning local words.

passage: In her first month at school in Chennai, Zeenat learned that her pink noon chai drew stares. 'Strawberry milk tea?' someone sniggered at break, and another girl copied the way she said 'ji' after everything. Zeenat started leaving the flask at home and answering in short English words only. On Saturday, walking past the Mylapore temple tank with Papa, she heard an old man teaching a child Tamil numbers, and found herself repeating them under her breath. On Monday she brought the flask back. When Lokesh from her bench asked what it was, she poured him a little. 'Salty? Pink? Weird,' he said, then took another sip. 'Actually good.' He taught her 'romba nalla', very good, and she taught him the Kashmiri word for tea. By Friday two more people wanted to try it, and Zeenat said 'ji' as often as she liked.

qa.q: What did Lokesh teach Zeenat to say?
qa.a: 'Romba nalla', very good.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat start leaving the flask at home?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and out of place after the sniggers, so she tried to hide what marked her as different.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Zeenat, and why?
qa.a: Bringing the flask back while also learning Tamil words, because she kept her roots and let an ally in 😊

qa.q: How does Lokesh see the noon chai?
qa.a: He finds it weird at first but is curious enough to taste it and decides it's actually good.

grounding: Shows a teen who moved to a new city and was teased for her language and food, keeping her roots, learning local ways and finding an ally.
